subject: pilot whale
title: This Whale Sprints at 20 mph Half a Mile Underwater, Where It Should Be Resting

scenes.text: Deep-diving whales move slowly to save oxygen. One of them does the opposite.
The short-finned pilot whale. Scientists off Tenerife glued sound and motion tags to 23 of them.
They dived to 1,000 metres. Most deep divers cruise there at one or two metres a second.
The pilot whales hit nine metres a second. Twenty miles an hour. Straight down, at the bottom of a 15-minute dive, in the dark.
The sprints lasted up to 79 seconds and burned up to a third of the dive's energy. The target was almost certainly big, fast squid.
The researchers called them the cheetahs of the deep sea. The chase happens where no one can watch it.

description:
Short-finned pilot whales tagged off Tenerife dived as deep as 1,018 metres and then sprinted at up to 9 metres a second, about 20 mph, at the deepest point of the dive.
Most deep-diving whales swim at 1 to 2 metres a second to save oxygen. The pilot whales' sprints lasted 19 to 79 seconds, used up to a third of the dive's locomotion energy, and were aimed at large, fast prey such as giant squid. The researchers called them the cheetahs of the deep sea.
What do you think they are chasing down there? Comment below.
first_comment: Pilot whales dive deeper by day and make more hunting buzzes at night, when the squid rise. Which ocean hunter should we tag next?
